title: Namdev
hook: a boy sets a bowl of milk before the god, and waits for him to drink

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jnaneshwar for the last time: the yogi on the tiger, the children on the willing wall, and a book that ends by asking good for all beings. Where did you skip the impressive entrance? Day nine hundred sixteen.
screen: `JNANESHWAR.` · `A WALL ONLY HAS TO BE WILLING.`

segments.voice: A bowl of milk sits on the floor of the temple at Pandharpur, in front of the image of Vitthal, the dark god who stands on a brick with his hands on his hips. A small boy has carried it there. His father usually brings the offering, but he's away, and today the boy has been sent instead. He sets it down, folds his hands, and waits. The god doesn't move. The milk doesn't move. The boy keeps waiting. Nobody has told him that offerings are usually received unseen. Today's saint is that boy: Namdev.
screen: `A BOWL OF MILK FOR VITTHAL.` → `A BOY SETS IT DOWN.` → `HE WAITS FOR THE GOD TO DRINK.`

segments.voice: Tradition says Namdev grew up in a family of tailors who were devoted to Vitthal, the form of Krishna worshiped at Pandharpur, whom his devotees call by tender names like Vithoba and, sometimes, mother. As the story goes, the boy waits, and still the god doesn't drink. So he begins to plead. He's done what his father does; why won't you take it? Is something wrong with me? Some tellings say he cries; some say he threatens to break his own head on the stone floor if Vitthal refuses. And Vitthal, the story says, reaches out of the image and drinks the milk. All of it. Then the boy goes home with an empty bowl, and nobody at home believes him. It's a funny story, and it knows it. But notice what it's saying. For Namdev, the god isn't an idea, and the offering isn't a gesture. If you bring a friend milk, the friend drinks it. He simply takes Vitthal at his word, the way a child takes anyone at their word. And the story doesn't correct him; it rewards him. Namdev grows up to be a singer. His songs, called abhangs, are short devotional poems, and in them he talks to Vitthal the way you'd talk to someone in the same room: pleading, teasing, complaining, longing. In the Varkari tradition, people still sing abhangs, Namdev's among them, in kirtan, call and response, with cymbals keeping the beat. Jnaneshwar gave the people the Gita in their own language. Namdev gives them something smaller and just as bold: permission to treat God like someone who might actually drink the milk.
screen: `A FAMILY OF TAILORS, DEVOTED TO VITTHAL.` · `WHY WON'T YOU TAKE IT?` · `VITTHAL DRINKS THE MILK.` · `ABHANGS: TALKING TO GOD IN THE ROOM.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably. Let your breath slow, and set your hands on your knees, palms up, as if you were holding a small bowl. Think of something simple you could offer today: a glass of water to someone, your full attention, a meal. Now offer it the way the boy did, as if it will really be received. Don't rush the waiting. If you pray, you can offer it to God, by Vitthal's name or any name you already use. The bell holds the time.
Namdev. The tailor's son of the Marathi saint tradition, who, the story says, waited until Vitthal drank the milk, and grew up singing abhangs.
Your line: the bowl of milk. Today, give one small thing and stay long enough to see it received. Day nine hundred sixteen.

howItsDone: Varkari devotees sing abhangs, including Namdev's, in kirtan with cymbals, and the temple of Vitthal at Pandharpur keeps a step at its entrance named for Namdev.

notes: Editor pass: hook no longer calls offerings 'just a ritual' (dismissive framing); 'the story wants you to laugh' softened.

Audit: the usual telling has his father (Damashet) as the one who normally made the offering, away that day, with Namdev sent in his place; hook and teach corrected from 'his mother usually brings it'. Disbelief now 'nobody at home'. 'The god isn't expected to drink' reworded (outsider framing of offering). Carry kept, though it echoes day 911's giving carry, because day 917's review depends on it.
All paraphrase. Confirm the milk story's details (sent by his mother; pleading; threat to strike his head in some tellings; Vitthal drinking; mother's disbelief).
Tradition varies on Namdev's birthplace (Pandharpur or Narsi); the script avoids naming it. Family of tailors (shimpi) attributed to tradition.
'Vitthal, the form of Krishna worshiped at Pandharpur' and 'sometimes, mother' (Vithu-mauli) — confirm phrasing.
Namdev's songs in the Guru Granth Sahib are left out here under the claims rule; day 917 could include them with a cited source.
